opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is actually a pretty interesting question, because the word "agent" has kind of been redefined over the last couple of years.

I come from a reinforcement learning background, and in RL, "agent" has a very precise meaning. It's the thing that interacts with an environment: it observes a state, takes an action, the environment changes, and you get some reward signal. The whole point is sequential decision-making. You care about the long-horizon consequences of your actions, not just whether one output looks good.

When people from the NLP community started talking about agents, especially after ChatGPT, I think their starting point was quite different. For a lot of them, an agent was basically a language model plus some prompting, plus some tools. You give the model a search API, a code interpreter, or a browser, you write a nice prompt, maybe you chain a few calls together in a workflow, and you call that an agent. In the early days, a lot of the "agent" papers were really prompt engineering or workflow design. The model itself wasn't trained to be an agent. It was a chatbot you wrapped in a loop.

That's not wrong, and it was actually a very practical way to get things working. But from my perspective it misses the core of what makes something an agent. If the model has never been trained on the consequences of its own actions in a multi-step environment, it doesn't really know how to plan, recover from mistakes, or explore. It's just predicting the next reasonable-looking response, one turn at a time.

What's changed recently, and I think this is the exciting part, is that the two views are converging. With models like o1 and DeepSeek-R1, people saw that you can use reinforcement learning on top of language models and get real reasoning ability out of it. Now the NLP community is increasingly saying: to get a good agent, you need to put the model in an environment, let it take many steps, use tools, and train it end-to-end with RL on outcomes. That's essentially going back to the RL definition of an agent, but with a language model as the policy.

So my short answer is that, for NLP researchers, "agent" originally meant a capability built from the outside, through prompts and tools and workflows. The more meaningful definition, which I think the field is moving toward, is a capability trained from the inside, a model that has actually learned to act in an environment over long horizons. That's also why I think agentic RL is one of the most important directions right now.

r001.rationale: The response says NLP researchers began talking about agents especially after ChatGPT, describing language models extended with tools and workflows such as search, code, and browsing.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a case of two communities arriving at the same word from very different directions, and the word now carries both meanings at once.

My own background is in reinforcement learning, and for us "agent" has always been a very precise, almost boring term. An agent is anything that sits inside a loop: it observes a state, takes an action, the environment responds, and it gets some reward signal. That's it. A chess program is an agent, a thermostat is an agent, a robot arm is an agent. The emphasis is on the interaction loop and on learning from the consequences of your own actions over time.

When people from the NLP side started using the word, around the time of ChatGPT and then AutoGPT, they meant something different and in some ways more ambitious. For them, an agent is essentially a large language model that has been given the ability to do things: call tools, browse the web, write and run code, break a task into steps, remember what it did earlier, and keep going without a human prompting every turn. The core object is still a language model. The "agent" part is the scaffolding around it: planning, tool use, memory, reflection.

So if you look at what each community is actually proud of, the RL people are proud of the learning algorithm, and the NLP people are proud of the base model's general capability. For a long time those didn't talk to each other much. A classic RL agent could learn beautifully within one environment but knew nothing about the world. A language-model agent knew a great deal about the world but, at least initially, wasn't really learning from its own actions at all. It was doing inference-time reasoning on top of a frozen model.

What I find interesting is that the two definitions are now converging. Once you take a language model, put it in a long-horizon environment, let it take many actions, and train it on the outcome, you're back to the RL definition. The reasoning models and the coding agents are exactly this: the NLP notion of an agent, trained with the RL notion of an agent. And I think that's the right way to understand the current usage. When an NLP researcher says "agent" today, they mostly mean a language model operating in a loop with tools and multi-step autonomy. Whether it's really an agent in my old sense depends on one question: is it actually learning from the consequences of those actions, or is it just a very articulate model following a script? Increasingly the answer is the former, and that's why the word finally fits.

r001.rationale: The response says NLP researchers started using “agent” around ChatGPT and AutoGPT for language models equipped to take actions such as using tools and writing code.

astra-6.text:
I think researchers coming from natural language processing often use “agent” to mean a language model that can do more than generate a response. You give it a task, and it can decide what to do next, call a tool, observe the result, and continue until it reaches an answer or completes the task. The language model becomes the decision-making component in a larger system.

That’s a somewhat different emphasis from the traditional reinforcement-learning perspective, where an agent is defined by its interaction with an environment: it receives observations, takes actions, and pursues an objective. From that perspective, an agent doesn’t necessarily need language at all.

So I see considerable overlap. What’s distinctive about today’s NLP usage is that language provides a common interface for instructions, reasoning, and tool use. But I’d distinguish a model’s ability to produce a plausible plan from a system’s ability to execute that plan, respond to feedback, and reliably finish the job. That interaction loop is the important part.

r001.rationale: The response says NLP researchers often use “agent” for a language model that can do more than generate a response, but it does not suggest that they first encountered the term when LLMs gained that capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think researchers from an NLP background often use “agent” to mean a language model that can do more than generate a response. It can take actions—call a tool, retrieve information, execute code—and then use the results to decide what to do next. So there’s a loop: observe, reason, act, and observe again.

That’s a little different from the traditional use in reinforcement learning, where an agent is broadly anything that interacts with an environment through observations and actions. From that perspective, the language model is one component of the agent, alongside things like memory and the interface to the environment.

So when someone says “agent,” I want to understand what decisions the system actually makes. Does it follow a fixed workflow, or can it choose its next action based on feedback? I think that distinction is more useful than the label itself.

r001.rationale: The candidate says NLP researchers use “agent” for language models that can act beyond generating responses, but does not say they may first encounter the term when models gain those capabilities.
